title: Cross-Lingual Disaster-related Multi-label Tweet Classification with Manifold Mixup
venue: Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Student Research Workshop (ACL 2020 SRW)
problem_statement: Social media provides critical situational awareness during disasters, but existing crisis NLP models focus predominantly on English tweets, lack standard large-scale multilingual multi-label disaster benchmarks, and cannot utilize partially labeled binary-annotated tweets alongside fine-grained multi-class data during training.
domain: Cross-lingual crisis informatics, disaster management, and multi-label social media (Twitter) text classification.
theoretical_framework: Manifold Mixup regularization theory (interpolating hidden state representations and target labels to induce linear behavior across representations), cross-lingual contextual representation learning via Multilingual BERT (M-BERT), and loss masking for partially supervised learning.
methodology: The authors aggregated six crisis datasets from CrisisNLP and CrisisLex into a unified multilingual corpus of over 130,000 tweets across five target classes (Informative, Casualties and Damage, Donation and Volunteering, Caution and Advice, and Non-Informative). To leverage both binary and fine-grained annotations without discarding partially labeled instances, the authors developed a masked binary cross-entropy loss function with class weighting. They fine-tuned Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) with Manifold Mixup—interpolating hidden states, ground-truth labels, and class masks across randomly selected transformer layers using mixing ratios sampled from a Beta(2, 2) distribution. They evaluated the proposed approach against FastText, CNN, XML-CNN, BiLSTM, Word Mixup, and Sentence Mixup across out-of-event test sets and zero-shot cross-lingual test sets in Spanish, French, and Italian.
datasets: Aggregated Multilingual Crisis Tweet Dataset: Over 130,000 tweets compiled from CrisisNLP (Resources #1, #4, #5, #7) and CrisisLex (CrisisLexT6, CrisisLexT26) covering English, French, Italian, Spanish, and other languages
Out-of-event Test Sets: Russia Meteor, Cyclone Pam, Philippines Flood, and Multilingual Mixed Disasters
key_findings: Multilingual BERT (M-BERT) significantly outperforms traditional deep learning sentence encoders (FastText, CNN, XML-CNN, and BiLSTM) across both out-of-event disaster tweet classification and multilingual benchmarks.

Applying Manifold Mixup to interpolate intermediate hidden representations in M-BERT consistently improves generalization across all test datasets, outperforming both Word Mixup and Sentence Mixup variants.

The class-masking loss formulation successfully leverages partially labeled binary crisis data alongside fine-grained multi-class data without discarding unannotated classes or impairing multi-label prediction capabilities.

M-BERT with Manifold Mixup demonstrates strong zero-shot cross-lingual transfer on unseen disaster languages, achieving F1-scores of 85.25% on Spanish, 81.33% on French, and 75.44% on Italian without any target-language training data.
The model achieves an F1-score exceeding 90% for identifying informative disaster tweets and retains competitive performance on low-frequency categories such as Caution and Advice.
scope_and_delimitations: Restricted dataset aggregation to textual content from six specific CrisisNLP and CrisisLex corpora, excluding image and multimodal features.

Delimited classification to four binary prediction heads (Informative vs. Non-Informative, Casualties and Damage, Caution and Advice, Donation and Volunteering) with positive classes treated as mutually exclusive during aggregation due to sparse multi-label source annotations.
Evaluated zero-shot cross-lingual generalization on three Romance languages (Spanish, French, Italian) present within M-BERT's 104 pretraining languages.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: Even though the classifiers are not mutually exclusive, the annotated classes (excluding the more general informative class) are kept mutually exclusive because there were not many multi-label annotations in the original data and most tweets tend to belong to only one of the specific classes. One could also use mutually exclusive classifiers with the given data.
limitations.summary: The authors acknowledge that the annotated classes were constrained to be mutually exclusive during dataset aggregation due to the scarcity of multi-label annotations in the source corpora. In addition, broader classes like Casualties and Damage combine diverse sub-categories to avoid class sparsity, and zero-shot cross-lingual capabilities remain bounded by the 104 languages covered during M-BERT pretraining.

generalizability_gap: The zero-shot cross-lingual capabilities were evaluated on three major European Romance languages (Spanish, French, Italian), leaving lower-resource languages, non-Indo-European languages, code-switched microblogs, and languages outside M-BERT's 104 pretraining languages untested.
methodological_gap: The dataset aggregation treats fine-grained positive classes as mutually exclusive due to historical annotation constraints, preventing the full exploration of true multi-label co-occurrences. Furthermore, the framework relies on heuristic class weighting and fixed Beta distribution parameters without exploring adaptive mixup schedules or weak supervision.
future_work: Exploring weak supervision techniques to automatically expand fine-grained multi-label disaster annotations.
Investigating additional data augmentation and regularization techniques to further improve model robustness in low-resource disaster settings.
Extending cross-lingual evaluation to diverse non-European and low-resource languages prone to natural disasters.
